findings.title: isAccessTokenId matcher checks the wrong characters and inverts the comparison
findings.body:
The new matcher is supposed to assert that an access-token id looks like `<session><token><grant>:<uuid>` and that the grant shortcut matches `expectedGrantShortcut`. Two defects make the check useless (and potentially wrong):

1. Wrong offset: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4 and 5 of the 6-char prefix (`on`+`rt`+`ac`), so it must be read with `substring(4, 6)`. `substring(3, 5)` reads the last char of the token-type plus the first char of the grant type (e.g. "ta" for "onrtac").
2. Inverted condition: `if (items[0].substring(3,5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` fails the match when the shortcut *equals* the expectation; it should be `if (!....equals(...)) return false;`.

Combined, the matcher currently always skips the grant check (the garbled 2-char slice never equals a real shortcut), so `expectCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken` and `expectAuthReqIdToToken` no longer verify anything about the encoded grant type — the main thing this PR introduces. Conversely, if `expectedGrantShortcut` ever happened to equal the garbled slice, every such assertion would fail. Additionally, `substring(3,5)` throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException (instead of returning false) for a prefix shorter than 5 chars, turning a mismatch into an error.

findings.title: New abstract getShortcut() breaks existing OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations
findings.body: `getShortcut()` is added to the `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` SPI interface without a `default` implementation. Any existing implementation of this SPI (third-party grant providers, and any grant factory in the repo/testsuite that was not updated in this PR) will no longer compile, and a pre-compiled provider JAR deployed into the server will fail at runtime. The failure is not localized to the grant itself: `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit()` iterates over *all* `OAuth2GrantType` factories, casts them to `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` and calls `getShortcut()`, so a single stale provider throws `AbstractMethodError` during server startup. Providing a `default` implementation (e.g. returning a neutral/unknown shortcut) and handling that value in the encoder would keep the SPI backwards compatible.

findings.title: Grant shortcut length is never validated, yet decoding hard-codes a 6-char prefix
findings.body: `getTokenContextFromTokenId()` requires the prefix before ':' to be exactly 6 characters (2 for session type + 2 for token type + 2 for grant type) and throws `IllegalArgumentException` otherwise, while `encodeTokenId()` happily concatenates whatever `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut()` returns. Nothing validates that a shortcut is exactly 2 characters — and the Javadoc of `getShortcut()` even states "usually like 3-letters shortcut", which actively invites 3-character values. A provider (or a future built-in grant) returning a shortcut of any other length will produce access-token IDs that this very provider can never decode, i.e. permanently undecodable tokens in the wild. Validate the shortcut length in `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit()` (fail fast at startup) and fix the Javadoc to state the exact required length.

findings.title: postInit can fail with a bare NPE if a grant factory returns a null shortcut
findings.body: `grantsByShortcuts`/`grantsToShortcuts` are `ConcurrentHashMap`s, which reject null keys and values. If any `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut()` implementation returns `null` (easy to do, since the method has no contract enforcing non-null), `postInit()` throws a `NullPointerException` from inside `ConcurrentHashMap.put`, aborting server startup with a message that gives no hint about which provider is at fault. An explicit null/length check with a descriptive `IllegalStateException` naming the offending factory id (similar to the existing duplicate-shortcut check below) would make the failure diagnosable.

findings.title: Copy-paste in constructor validation leaves rawTokenId unchecked
findings.body: `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` checks `grantType` for the second time instead of `rawTokenId`. As a result a `null` raw token id passes validation and later produces an access-token id literally ending in ":null" (`encodeTokenId` concatenates it), instead of failing fast at construction. The message is also misleading if `grantType` is the actual null argument. Should be `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, ...)`.

findings.title: Session type derived from client session instead of the user session used for the token
findings.body: The provider resolves the session type via `clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getUserSession()`, while `TokenManager.initToken` already has the authoritative `UserSessionModel` parameter that the rest of token creation uses (subject, session id, persistence state). Any code path that builds a `ClientSessionContext` whose client session is not (yet) attached to a user session, or where the passed `userSession` differs from the one on the client session, will either NPE during token issuance or encode the wrong session type into every access token of that flow. Passing the `userSession` already available in `initToken` into `getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext` removes this divergence.

findings.title: Decoding a malformed token id throws instead of degrading to UNKNOWN
findings.body: `getTokenContextFromTokenId()` returns an all-UNKNOWN context for ids without ':' (legacy tokens), but throws `IllegalArgumentException` for ids that contain ':' with an unexpected prefix length or unknown shortcuts. Token ids come from client-supplied tokens (the stated goal is to call this from introspection/userinfo/admin endpoints), so once wired up any crafted or foreign `jti` turns into an unhandled runtime exception, i.e. an HTTP 500 instead of an invalid-token response. Treating unparseable prefixes the same way as legacy ids (UNKNOWN context) or wrapping the call in explicit error handling at the call sites is needed before these endpoints start consuming it.

findings.title: Format change of access-token jti is not documented in upgrading/release notes
findings.body: Access tokens no longer carry a plain UUID in `jti`; the value becomes `<6 chars>:<uuid>` (and `Details.TOKEN_ID` in events changes accordingly). This is an externally visible, behaviour-changing contract: resource servers, log/SIEM pipelines and client libraries that parse or store `jti` as a UUID (fixed 36-char column, `UUID.fromString(...)`) will break on upgrade. The PR contains no upgrading/release-note documentation for this change, nor any statement that the prefix is opaque and must not be relied upon by third parties.

findings.title: Negative test accepts any RuntimeException and ignores the result
findings.body: `testIncorrectGrantType` catches `RuntimeException`, so the test would also pass if the code threw an unrelated `NullPointerException` instead of the intended `IllegalArgumentException` about an unknown grant shortcut; the declared `ctx` variable is unused. Assert the expected exception type (and ideally the message) so the test actually pins the contract of `getTokenContextFromTokenId`.

findings.title: No test coverage for the context values actually encoded during token issuance
findings.body: The only tests are unit tests that decode hand-written token ids; nothing verifies the mapping performed by `getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext`, i.e. that an offline-session token really gets `of`, a transient session `tr`, a lightweight access token `lt`, and that the grant-type attribute is populated for every grant that now sets `Constants.GRANT_TYPE` (authorization code, refresh, password, token exchange, pre-authorized code, device, CIBA). Given that the AssertEvents matcher that was supposed to cover this in integration tests is broken (grant check never executes), the whole encoding path is effectively untested end to end.
